case_name: Tipon v. Fleet Brake Parts & Service Limited
text:
In the Provincial Court of Alberta

Citation: Tipon
v. Fleet Brake Parts & Service Limited, 2017 ABPC 29

Date:
20170210

Docket:
P1590304206

Registry:
Edmonton

Between:

Dindo I. Tipon

Plaintiff

- and -

Fleet Brake Parts & Service Limited

Defendant

Reasons for Judgment of the
Honourable
Judge

J.L. Skitsko

[
1
]

Fleet Brake Parts & Services Limited (“Fleet
Brake” or the “Defendant” or the “employer”) formally dismissed Mr. Dindo I.
Tipon (the “Plaintiff” or the “employee”) on May 27, 2015 after four years of
service. The Plaintiff commenced this action on August 13, 2015 for damages
flowing from an alleged wrongful dismissal.

[
2
]

The issues in this case are:

A)

Did the Defendant wrongfully dismiss the Plaintiff?

i.

Can the Defendant rely on “after acquired
cause”?

B)

Did the Defendant dismiss the Plaintiff in bad faith?

FACTS

Overview

[
3
]

Mr. Tipon’s responsibilities at Fleet Brake
included maintaining the company’s “COR” (Certificate of Recognition)
certification. This designation recognizes a high standard of
industrial/commercial safety and thereby creates several associated benefits
for companies that maintain certification.

[
4
]

Ultimately, Fleet Brake lost its COR
certification and subsequently summarily dismissed Mr. Tipon. It provided Mr.
Tipon one month’s salary as severance pay.

[
5
]

The circumstances of Mr. Tipon’s employment in
the period prior to the loss of Fleet Brake’s COR certification are important,
and include the following:

•

Mr. Tipon was ill and Fleet Brake was aware of
his illness;

•

Mr. Tipon’s immediate supervisor left the
company. Replacement supervision was provided by a Vice-President located in
Calgary whom had minimal contact with Mr. Tipon;

•

Fleet Brake hired, then subsequently terminated,
an assistant for Mr. Tipon;

•

Fleet Brake was rapidly expanding its operations
in Alberta.

COR Certification

[
6
]

A COR designation gives a company significant
credibility as a leader in high safety standards. Further, it is a prerequisite
to serving certain clientele, such as the municipalities of Edmonton and
Calgary, and creates significant reductions in WCB premiums. In the past, Fleet
Brake has saved over $20,000 during the course of one year in COR associated
WCB discounts.

[
7
]

A COR certification requires that thorough and
onerous safety audits are performed both internally and externally.
Additionally, COR designated companies cannot “sit on their laurels”.  They
must stay alert to safety issues within their company, and maintain ongoing
records.

[
8
]

Employees such as Mr. Tipon monitor company
safety practices and perform the necessary internal audit. An audit requires
personal interviews of all workers at each of a company’s various locations.
The questions asked follow strict checklists and interviews must be conducted
within strict timelines.  Once information from an internal audit is obtained
and reviewed, it submitted to an authorized third party.

[
9
]

These non-biased third parties, such as the Workers’
Compensation Board of Alberta (“WCB”) and the Manufacturers’ Health and Safety
Association (“MHSA”) perform the necessary external audit.

[
10
]

The standards required for COR certification are
uniform, and have proven to be very rigid in their application. Overall, the
collection, review, and production of information to external auditors can
create an imposing challenge for companies seeking certification. One strict
requirement is the date an external auditor receives an application for an
audit. The designated date in this case was December 31, 2014.

Evidence of Dindo Tipon

Viva voce evidence

[
11
]

Mr. Tipon immigrated to Canada from the
Philippines in March of 2006.   He was educated as an engineer in the
Phillipines, but did not have the necessary qualifications to practice as an
engineer in Alberta.

[
12
]

He first began working for an associated company
of the Defendant, Peerless Parts and Service (“Peerless”), in April of 2011.
This company eventually merged with the Defendant. It is not in dispute that Mr.
Tipon provided just over 4 years of service to the Defendant.

[
13
]

Peerless originally hired Mr. Tipon as a Safety
Training Officer.  His role was to manage the safety requirements of all
Alberta offices, including conducting internal audits for COR certification. When
he started with the company, there were four offices in Alberta.

[
14
]

Mr. Tipon’s evidence made it clear that the
company was growing.  Four additional branch offices became part of his
workload in his last year of service. This created a significant increase in
his responsibilities.

[
15
]

When Mr. Tipon was only responsible for the
original four company offices, he worked closely with one of the company’s
Vice-Presidents, Mr. Shawn Johns.  The two met on a daily basis.  I am
satisfied that Mr. Johns was extremely helpful to Mr. Tipon and assisted him in
completing his tasks on a timely basis.

[
16
]

Mr. Tipon described the kind of help he received
from Mr. Johns.  Mr. Johns advised him regarding the entire COR process, its
importance to the company, and the extent of the hands-on work expected.  Mr. Johns
impressed upon Mr. Tipon that the work was ongoing throughout the year.  The
process was not “an overnight thing”.  It required months of preparation and regular
data collection, as well as reviews of the information and presentation in
formats acceptable to external auditors.

[
17
]

Mr. Johns was also responsible for Mr. Tipon’s annual
performance reviews. Mr. Johns completed employment performance reviews of Mr.
Tipon in 2012 and 2013. These reviews were both satisfactory.

[
18
]

In early January of 2014, Mr. Tipon became very
ill with an autoimmune disease known as “
lichen planus
”.  This disorder
affects different people in different ways. The disease attacked his skin,
spleen, and gums, and proved to be very debilitating. He suffered from
resultant sleep deprivation, which affected  his energy level, stamina, and
memory. Accordingly, at various times he was not able to work for up to a full
work week.

[
19
]

Mr. Tipon’s treatment began in early 2014.  It
consisted of a heavy intake of steroids.  Recovery was slow.  It took a
significant period of time for the medications to provide him with any kind of
relief. Mr. Tipon advised the Court that the medications he was taking made him
irritable and impatient.

[
20
]

Mr. Tipon advised Mr. Johns of his disease in
early February.  I find that Mr. Johns appointed an assistant to work alongside
Mr. Tipon in order to accommodate Mr. Tipon’s illness.  This assistant was
Neide Jurace.  She assumed some of Mr. Tipon’s duties.

[
21
]

Mr. Johns subsequently had a falling out with
the company and left in March of 2014.  The Plaintiff testified, as was confirmed
by the testimony of Mr. Johns, that Mr. Johns left because he did not agree
with the Defendant’s aggressive expansion plan. This plan would see the company
double its number of branches that year.

[
22
]

After Mr. Johns’ departure, Mr. Mel Palma, a
Vice-President of Fleet Brake’s Calgary office, became Mr. Tipon’s immediate
supervisor.  This was a significant change, as Mr. Tipon would no longer
interact with his supervisor on a daily basis.  There were now only two
corporate employees left in the Edmonton office: the Plaintiff and his
assistant, Ms. Jurace.

[
23
]

By April of 2014,  it was clear that Mr. Palma
would not be in a position to interact regularly with Mr. Tipon.  Mr. Palma was
located in Calgary and  his contact with Mr. Tipon was minimal.  I am satisfied
that personal assistance and mentoring was non-existent under this
arrangement.  The Plaintiff told the Court he may have met with Mr. Palma three
times over the following year.

[
24
]

One of Mr. Palma’s responsibilities was to conduct
Mr. Tipon’s employment reviews.  However, he did not conduct any such reviews.
Mr. Tipon’s most recent employment review was the review conducted by Mr. Johns
in 2013.

[
25
]

Mr. Palma was not called as a witness to explain
why this was the case.  Further, Fleet Brake provided the Court with no
explanation for Mr. Palma’s absence as a witness.

[
26
]

By late March 2014, circumstances within the
company began to spin wildly out of control from Mr. Tipon’s perspective.  Mr.
Johns had left the company.  Mr. Tipon saw his workload increase dramatically,
as Fleet Brake opened four new branch offices in addition to the four branches that
were already operational in Alberta.

[
27
]

Mr. Tipon knew that the new branches would add a
significant amount of work to his responsibilities.  This coupled with his
illness and his reduced energy levels made it essential that he get help.  I am
satisfied that Mr. Johns knew this, and this is why he appointed Ms. Jurace as
the Plaintiff’s assistant.

[
28
]

Ms. Jurace took on some of Mr. Tipon’s
responsibilities: all safety related issues of the Edmonton office were
delegated to her. This responsibility made Ms. Jurace very busy in both
learning the job and collecting information.

[
29
]

Mr. Tipon took a medical vacation to travel to
the Philippines in late spring of 2014. While there, he took further treatments
and detoxification in order to battle his
lichen planus
.

[
30
]

When Mr. Tipon returned to work on May 26, 2014,
he assumed a modified work schedule.  He was no longer travelling between the
various branches of the offices in Alberta.  However, he continued to work
full-time, with his focus now on managing Fleet Brake’s WCB claims.  He advised
that during this time, Ms. Jurace was completing all external workplace audits
and reporting to him.  I am satisfied that Ms. Jurace was providing key
assistance to Mr. Tipon.

[
31
]

By the end of the summer months of 2014, Mr.
Tipon assessed Ms. Jurace’s help as important, professional and timely.

[
32
]

On September 18, 2014, Mr. Palma issued a
directive to Mr. Tipon – he had to fire Ms. Jurace.

[
33
]

Mr. Tipon attempted to talk Mr. Palma out of
dismissing Ms. Jurace.  Mr. Tipon viewed her as indispensable.  In his
uncontradicted evidence, Mr. Tipon told the Court he told Mr. Palma that firing
Mr. Jurace at this time was, in his view, a very bad idea, as he could not
possibly complete the audit without her assistance.  Mr. Tipon advised Mr.
Palma that if Ms. Jurace was dismissed, the company would be placed in a very
difficult position, and might not be capable of passing COR external audits on
a timely basis.

[
34
]

Mr. Tipon also advised Mr. Palma that he would
not be able to work toward the COR audit for the balance of September 2014 and
at least part of the month of October 2014, as he was very heavily occupied
with processing WCB safety claims.

[
35
]

Notwithstanding his protestations, Mr. Tipon
followed Mr. Palma’s direction and dismissed Ms. Jurace on September 24, 2014.

[
36
]

After September 24, 2014, Mr. Tipon was the only
corporate employee left in Edmonton. He was responsible for processing WCB
safety claims, and coordinating the COR for each Alberta branch of Fleet Brake.

[
37
]

It was also clear in his evidence that Mr.
Tipon’s medical condition had not improved by the fall of 2014.

[
38
]

By the late fall of 2014, the MHSA
representative asked the Plaintiff to provide the necessary information for the
external COR audit by December.

[
39
]

When MHSA made this request, Mr. Tipon made it
clear to MHSA that he could not possibly meet the December deadline and he asked
for an extension.  In response, MHSA asked for a medical report on his current
condition, which they advised they would consider in reviewing his request for
an extension.

[
40
]

I find Mr. Tipon naively believed he could work
hard enough to meet the COR requirements before the end of the year, or he
would get an extension and it would all work out.  Naiveté is not dishonesty.  I
find he honestly believed that he would obtain this extension of time.

[
41
]

Mr. Tipon advised the Court that he “believed”
he had sent some e-mails to Mr. Palma about his medical condition, and his
inability to meet audit deadlines set by the MHSA.

[
42
]

The application for the audit extension was
ultimately rejected on March 27, 2015.

[
43
]

On May 27, 2015, Mr. Tipon returned from his spring
vacation in the Phillipines. He was dismissed by Mr. Bzeta, the employer’s
President.

[
44
]

At the time of his termination, Mr. Tipon was
earning $82,400.00 per annum.  He may have been eligible for a bonus.  In 2013,
Mr. Tipon was paid $13,000.00  under his bonus plan.

[
45
]

Mr. Tipon received four weeks, or one month, of
salary in lieu of his severance.  He received no profit sharing or bonus
amount.  No further RRSP contributions and no vacation pay or health benefits
were advanced to him in lieu of his dismissal.

[
46
]

It took Tipon 4.5 months to find alternate
work.  His new job paid him $57,000.00 per year along with some health
benefits.  His 2014 T4 summaries indicated employment income of $94,211.70.  I
note his 2013 income totalled $87,846.00 and his 2012 income totalled
$78,320.00.  In each of those three years, Mr. Tipon admitted to receiving
various amounts of bonuses with the 2013 $13,000.00 bonus being the largest.

[
47
]

The Plaintiff admitted he is not certified as a
safety auditor.  He was in the process of being evaluated in this area prior to
his termination.  He believed that Ms. Jurace was also working towards her
safety audit training.

Documentary
Evidence

[
48
]

Counsel for Mr. Tipon put into evidence Exhibit
1, a binder containing dozens of electronic communications, letters, and
correspondence drafted or received by Mr. Tipon (the “binder”). Another binder
also containing dozens of documents was put into evidence as Exhibit 5.  I
reviewed each and every document therein.

[
49
]

On August 14, 2014, Mr. Tipon made it clear to
Anita Valdezco, the Human Relations Supervisor, that he was extremely busy with
pre-internal audit meetings.

[
50
]

On September 16, 2014, in a letter copied to Mr.
Palma and Mr. Tim Douglas, Mr. Tipon pointed out five areas that would be
audited in the first quarter of 2015 (appointment maintenance and inspection
records, monthly inspection reports, incident investigation reports, minutes of
meetings, and HAA Policy Review and Training Record).  All of these would need
to be provided to an external auditor on a timely basis.

[
51
]

On September 19, 2014, letter from Donna Chymko
at WCB, addressed to Mr. Palma and copied to Mr. Tipon, verified what part of
the COR certification process was intended to accomplish: a reduction of WCB
premiums. The letter made it clear that with COR certification, a refund of
$19,443.00 from WCB could be expected in the next fiscal year.

[
52
]

On April 3, 2014, Mr. Tipon forwarded an e-mail
to Ms. Valdezco in Human Relations wherein he indicated to her that he was in
the hospital and that he was dealing with pain that was “too much.”

[
53
]

On April 7, 2014, Mr. Tipon sent an e-mail to
Ms. Valdezco, Mr. Palma and Mr. Douglas.  It read:

“From Dindo Tipon
sent April 4, 2014 to Mel Palma and Tim Douglas with a carbon to Anita Valdezco

Subject:  Update

Hi Mel and Tim.  Just
finished a medical evaluation by doctors of University of Alberta, good [sic]
thing is that no other complications seen for my current health issues.  I can
go for [sic] work on Tuesday as they advised me to stay home and minimize
walking in the next three days from Saturday to Monday.”

[
54
]

Other e-mails sent to Mr. Palma during the month
of April 2014 made it absolutely clear that Mr. Palma was aware Mr. Tipon was
experiencing health issues. It was also clear that Mr. Tipon continued with
doctor and other medical appointment dates for May 27, July 10, July 11, July
24, July 28, July 29, August 21, September 8, September 23, and September 29.

[
55
]

On September 6, 2014, Mr. Tipon sent a general
e-mail message to no less than 24 employees of Fleet Brake.  The letter made it
very clear that he continued to exhibit every intention of completing the audit
with Ms. Jurace’s assistance.  The letter to this significant group referenced
his discussion with the third party safety auditors and Mr. Tipon instructed
all to review their records in five areas.

[
56
]

Incredibly, on September 18, 2014, during a
meeting with Mr. Palma, Mr. Tipon was instructed to dismiss Ms. Jurace.

[
57
]

On October 9, 2014 Mr. Tipon sent a letter to
the management of branch 9 of Fleet Brake:

“I did not
receive the investigation report for the incidents listed in our tracking
system which I emailed to you last week ... In the future if this is not
corrected then I have no choice but indicate [sic] in our corporate safety
monthly report that “the branch failed to do the investigation report”  There
are 2 negative effects if you are not going to do this thing on time, non
compliance with OH & S legislation and major deviation of COR practice.”

[
58
]

On December 10, 2014, Mr. Tipon sent a letter to
one of the COR “outside” administrators, Crystal Gaudet, with the following
information:

“Subject Re: Audit Submissions due by
December 31

I might be having a problem with the
target date.  Can I send a letter of request to extend it since some of our
managers are on holidays next week?”

[
59
]

The response, also dated December 10, read:

“Unfortunately we are unable to extend
the submission date.  This is something that is set out by partnerships [a
group of industry standards consultants who meet and collectively set safety
standards] that we have to follow.”

[
60
]

Shortly thereafter, Mr. Tipon e-mailed Ms.
Gaudet with the following:

“Subject Re: August Submissions Due by
December 31

What will happen if we miss this internal
audit, we are set to do one actually this March 2015?”

[
61
]

Ms. Gaudet’s response was on December 11 and
read:

“Hi Dindo,

You will lose your COR if an audit is not
submitted.  Also please keep in mind that there must be a minimum of 6 months
between an internal and external audit.”

[
62
]

Mr. Tipon, relying on his personal skills and
past relationships, called one of the occupational health and safety (“OHS”)
officers, Mr. Jeffrey Smith, in order to seek an extension.  Mr. Smith wrote to
him on December 12, 2014:

“Hi Dindo,

Good to talk to you.  I am glad you are
getting healthy from that scare.

I’m copying Jamie Simpson, he’s the parthership’s
consultant who works with MHSA.  There is no specific process on requesting an
exception to existing partnerships standards – b
ut typically certifying partners
approach our management with written and detailed
requests on
behalf of individual employers.  Our director then makes a decision on each
case based on its own merits.  In your case, work with MHSA on how your serious
illness affected Fleet Brakes ability to complete a maintenance audit in 2014.

Continue to work with MHSA and document your
request.  When you are ready – have MHSA approach Jamie who can then take the
request to our director for a decision.”

[
63
]

The contents of this e-mail was revealing.  Mr.
Smith did not say “No” to the request.  He did however, reference conditions
that were beyond his control. It seems to me that in reading the above e-mail
from Mr. Smith, copied to the OHS Director, that it is the OHS Director who
decides if an extension will be granted on a case-by-case basis.  This is
significant, because according to the evidence presented by the Defendant,
extension requests for COR audits were never provided.  In this letter, Mr. Tipon
was provided with some hope that the OHS Director could make a decision to
extend Fleet Brake’s deadline.

[
64
]

Mr. Smith followed up with a second letter on
January 22, 2015.  The letter made it clear that Mr. Tipon would have to work
through the MHSA and prepare a written and detailed request for a “partnerships
standards” exception.  Mr. Smith’s supervisor, Mr. Simpson, would then take
that request to the OHS Director who would make the decision on the extension
application, as neither Mr. Smith nor Mr. Simpson had authority to extend the
deadline.

[
65
]

Mr. Tipon requested an extension from MHSA,
which was answered by Ms. Luba Smidlehner of MHSA on February 17, 2015.

“My name is Luba and I work in the COR
department for the MHSA.  With respect to the extension request, please provide
detailed information as to why the extension was needed.  Ensure to include
dates and any supporting documents such as doctor’s notes that can substantiate
why the extension was needed.  Please send this directly to me and once it is
received I will forward it off to our partnership consultant for review. Should
you have any questions please contact me directly.”

[
66
]

After receiving an explanation of his medical
issues, Ms. Smidlehner responded to Mr. Tipon with these questions on February
18, 2015:

1.

Due to the severity of your illness, why
did you wait so long to having [sic] another individual take the training?

2.

When did Nadia [sic] Jurace leave
exactly? Did you contact MHSA?  If not, why?

3.

Did you have any other conversations with
MHSA staff members?

4.

At any time did MHSA staff provide
alternatives to having the 2014 audit completed?

[
67
]

Mr. Tipon’s response was two minutes later.  It
reads verbatim:

“Just to let you know
what happened to me last 2014 and was started last week of January when I was
given a wrong prescription by the doctor.  After 3 days of taking it I started
to get ill and had a severe coughing.  Then first week of February I have
noticed that my skin on my feet were peeling off.  Then I was diagnosed with
Lichen Planus.  My doctor did a short term steroids treatment but it did not
work.  I lost my hair and suffered severe skin eruption which makes me
difficult to sleep and walk and at that time too the pharmacist gave me a wrong
dosage of steroids which ended up in a dispute at the Provincial Court.

When I had a severe
skin eruption on my genital parts I decided to go to the Grey Nuns Hospital on
April 1st but then they referred me to the University of Alberta Hospital.  I
was given steroids for three months ... at that time I suffered from steroid
side effects such as fluid retention in my body which makes me difficult to
breathe, limited sleep (two hours a day) got easily irritated and others.  ...
After taking the steroids I had a bit of a problem of my memory and still
difficulty in breathing.

When I started to
feel better on September I sent our branch assistant, Neide Jurace for Safety
Auditors Course in order for her to do internal audit for us but unfortunately
she left on the same month after her training.  At that time I am not yet fully
recovered, I consulted again my doctor cause I am having difficulties in
walking and was worried cause I am thinking the side effect of steroids to my
bones.

Month of December
when I received an e-mail from MHSA saying that we have to submit the audit
report.  At first I asked that the internal audit report is to be done a year
before the external since I forgot the rules (perhaps due to what I am
experiencing) and so I received a reply from MHSA.  Then I asked the assistance
of MHSA if they could do internal audit for us on March 2015 since I will be on
holidays from January 23 to February 13.  Part of my holiday plan is to undergo
some treatment outside of Canada.

I will be forwarding
to you a medical certification tomorrow since my doctor is on duty tonight.
Meanwhile please see attached picture. ...”

[
68
]

Mr. Tipon then followed up with another response
on February 18
th
.   It reads verbatim:

“Hi Luba,

To answer your
questions I almost forgot everything last year.  I am so worried about my
health, especially when the doctor told me that if the steroids will not work
shutting off my immune system then I have to undergo chemo and at that time and
I got easily irritated.  My family doctor will tell you that my decision making
is no good at all (I saw him yesterday and he will release a medical
certification this week).  From February to November 2014, you can consider me
as unproductive worker (my intellectual ability is nothing).  My memory was not
good at all and have difficulties in doing physical activities since I am
suffering fluid retention at my feet.

Before my illness
became severe I have already programed Nadia’s training[sic] and so what she
did is to enrol herself to the class.
At that time I have no idea that the
corporate office will going to terminate her and I was just only inform on the
18th of September and her last day of work was September 25
th
.
I
was undergoing series of medical evaluations which started September after I
finished the steroids program.  I had my weekly bloodwork (I think 2 times a
week) where it was  very painful one on my part since I have very thin skin due
to the side effects of the drugs.  I took an phlebotomist use a butterfly tube
in order to extract blood and not to cause bruises.  I had my vital organs
check also during those months and, on month of November an ENT specialist had
inserted tubes to my nose to see what’s going on to my throat.  So much busy
and tired of all those tests.

I did not
contact MHSA since my priority is to finish all medical evaluations and
treatments (Nadia [sic] was gone at that time).  There were lots of things
happening, including the Court case against the pharmacist who dispensed the
wrong dosage of steroids and my apartment got robbed where my jewellers were
stolen amounting to $12,000.00 last November too. (You have verify this with
EPS and my insurance provider).  Then month of December I moved to new condo
that I bought.” [Emphasis added]

[
69
]

Included in this chain of discussions with MHSA
was a March 3, 2015 letter from Mr. Tipon’s doctor, Dr. Moustafa Mami.  Dr.
Mami was not called as a witness.

[
70
]

However, Dr. Mami’s letter explained Mr. Tipon
experienced a severe reaction to medication in January of 2014. The peak of the
adverse reaction occurred during the months of March 2014 through August 2014.
The note ends “during the past period of time Mr. Tipon was not able to make
clear decisions and his sickness affected his work performance”.

[
71
]

It is noteworthy that during the process of
substantiating Mr. Tipon’s request for an extension, by March 17, 2015, Ms.
Smidlehner had still not received official word as to whether the extension
application was to be granted.

[
72
]

On March 23, 2015, Mr. Tipon wrote to Mr. Ben
Smith, the Service Manager of the Defendant located at Branch 1.  He wrote in
part that:

“... we still
have lots of time to prepare.  MHSA is just only waiting for the confirmation
for advice from Alberta Human Services to one of the partners in the
partnership in Injury Reduction.”

[
73
]

On March 24, 2015, Tim Douglas wrote to Mr.
Tipon and copied Mr. Palma, Mr. Bzeta and Branch 1’s Mr. Sumka. Mr. Douglas’ letter
clearly referenced frustrations with one of the Defendant’s branches, “Branch
9”.  The branch was noted to be “somewhat” behind schedule.  Branch 9 was one
of those branches absorbed by the Defendant during expansion in 2014.  The
letter reads as follows:

“I am sure you [Mr. Tipon] know that
Branch 9 is struggling currently to meet its monthly budget and is striving to
build every hour and sell every part.  ...  We executive are putting pressure
on Walter and Corey to increase business back up to former levels and expect
the same from next year’s budget.  As such, they are reluctant to pull income
earning staff off the floor.

While it is obviously impossible to
fulfill all safety functions at all branches, we expect you to do so at Branch
9.  Here is the list you sent to Corey:

1.
Minutes of monthly toolbox meeting

2.
Worksite EHS monthly inspection
summary

3.
Updating training records

4.
Updating bulletin board

5.
Filing all safety records except
WCB

6.
Orientation of new employee”

[
74
]

This letter demonstrated and confirmed that other
glaring company deficiencies would have prevented a successful COR application,
independent of Mr. Tipon’s alleged incompetence.  One of the branches of the
Defendant was not prepared to assign branch staff to assist the COR audit
coordinator to complete his audit on a timely basis. Branch 9 remained in
default of reporting requirements six months after the strongly worded request
from Mr. Tipon on October 9, 2014.

[
75
]

Confirmation of this was provided in a March 25,
2015 letter by Mr. Tipon to Mr. Palma and Mr. Douglas.  It stated:

“Hi
Mel and Tim,

Inasmuch
as I would like to do all the safety stuff for Branch 9, unfortunately there is
no assurance that I will be in the branch most of the time.  I don’t want to
say yes but in the end there is no result.  Some of the action items identified
need 100% presence of the person like taking minutes of the meeting and
recording the inspection results.  All branches are doing their own except for
Branch 9 who are relying on me to do it for them.  When Neide left I had a
meeting with these 3 branch managers telling them what can I do and what I
can’t do for them.

ANALYSIS

[
161
]

I am satisfied that when Mr. Tipon began his employment with the
company on April 6, 2011, his work entailed the management of 4 branches across
the province of Alberta.  In 2012 and 2013, as part of his responsibilities,
Mr. Tipon travelled extensively to the various branches as part of his duties.
I am satisfied that at least until he became ill, he performed his work well.

[
162
]

Mr. Tipon was employed by the Defendant in a significant position of
responsibility.  He was given the job of collecting, reviewing, and submitting
all internal safety information to external auditors.  He was earning $6,867.00
per month at dismissal.  He may have been entitled to a bonus but did not lead
evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, he was entitled to receive a
bonus.

[
163
]

Courts are reminded in
McKinely v BC Tel
,
2001, SCC 38
, that
we must look at the history of an employee’s duties and responsibilities to
provide context to an employer’s allegations of just cause. In this case, the
allegation was that Mr. Tipon not only failed to complete his COR
recertification duties, but also that he deceived the employer regarding the
state of the company’s prospects for COR recertification.

[
164
]

The facts reveal that Mr. Shawn Johns was instrumental to Mr. Tipon’s
early success and the company’s initial COR certification. Mr. Johns met
regularly with Mr. Tipon, as both worked in the company’s Edmonton office.

[
165
]

Mr. Johns, as the one responsible for each of the Defendant’s safety
programs, told the Court that Mr. Tipon performed very well.  After listening
to Mr. Johns’ evidence, it became very clear to me that Mr. Tipon’s work was
extremely detailed.  Mr. Tipon would meet with all employees of all branches,
interview them on safety issues, evaluate their safety performances,  and
suggest various levels of improvement.

[
166
]

After the company’s first successful COR certification, I am
satisfied that the company began to take a different direction.  The company
began to expand and take on more employees.  Mr. Johns opposed this rapid expansion,
and related his opposition to this decision as the reason why Fleet Brake
dismissed him from the company in early March of 2014.  It was his opinion that
the company was “moving too quickly” and because, as he put it, he “raised
hell”, a parting of ways with the executive members of the company became
inevitable.

[
167
]

Fleet Brake’s acquisition of new business operations across the province
added significantly to Mr. Tipon’s responsibilities.  More assistance was
required.  Mr. Johns at least initially ensured Mr. Tipon received help.

[
168
]

Further, in January of 2014, Mr. Tipon became ill.  His illness was
not diagnosed for a significant period of time.  He began to miss work and,
especially given the added branches, work began to pile up.  I am satisfied that,
notwithstanding the illness, Mr. Tipon missed relatively few work days after
February 2014, the onset of his illness.

[
169
]

With Mr. Johns’ departure Mr. Tipon lost a mentor and a friend. In
2013, Mr Johns  guided Mr. Tipon through the process leading up to the COR
certification. I am satisfied Mr. Johns’ departure had a significant impact on Mr.
Tipon’s ability to successfully complete his work.  The work piled up.

[
170
]

Notwithstanding the fact that Mr. Johns put Ms. Jurace in a position
to assist Mr. Tipon, I am satisfied Mr. Tipon needed more assistance than she
was able to provide.

Was Mr. Tipon Wrongfully
Dismissed?

[
171
]

An employer who dismisses an employee summarily must prove on a
balance of probabilities that it had “just cause” to terminate his or her
employment.

[
172
]

Fleet Brake admits it summarily dismissed Mr. Tipon, despite providing
him with four weeks’ worth of wages in lieu of the dismissal. It asserted Mr.
Tipon could be summarily dismissed on the following grounds:

1.

Mr. Tipon’s competence fell well below the
standard that the employer could reasonably expect as part of its employment
contract. Mr. Tipon failed to property perform his duties as a safety officer,
causing the employer to lose its COR certification.

2.

Mr. Tipon failed to disclose the status of the
COR certification deadline, and the amount of associated work remaining during
the time leading up to the deadline, and in fact deceived or misled the company
to believe that the COR recertification application was in the process of being
approved.

[
173
]

Ultimately, the employer argued that the
employee’s performance was substandard and was “... conduct which goes to the
root of the contract and fundamentally strikes at the employment relationship”
(see Panton v. Everywoman’s Health Center Society (1988),
2000 BCCA 621
).

[
174
]

Since
McKinley, supra,
trial courts have adopted the
“contextual approach” in determining whether the conduct of an employee
provides cause for dismissal.  As Justice Iacobucci stated at para. 29:

“Within
this analysis, a finding of misconduct does not, by itself, give rise to just
cause.  Rather, the question to be addressed is whether, in the circumstances,
the behaviour was such that the employment relationship could no longer viably
subsist.”

[
175
]

At paragraph 33 of
McKinley
, the Supreme Court cited the
reasoning of the Nova Scota Court of Appeal in
Blackburn
v.
Victory
Credit Union
(1998)
1998 CanLII 6089 (NS CA)
, 36  CCEL (2d) 94 [
Blackburn
] with approval.  In
Blackburn
,
at p. 124 Flinn JA stated:

“What
constitutes just cause in a specific situation is particularly difficult to
enumerate because it depends not only on the category and possible consequences
of the misconduct, but also on both the nature of the employment and status of
the employee ...”

[
176
]

As an extension of this, I believe courts must also look at the
extent of involvement of the employer in the employee’s workplace.  It seems to
me that when an employer alleges that the employee lacked the competence to
complete the work, the employer must have been in a position to regularly review
the work of the employee so as to be in a position to judge the competence of
the work.

[
177
]

Competent supervisors will provide instruction, advice, correction,
and discipline, if necessary, on a regular, if not daily, basis.  Regular
supervision will give the employee the greatest chance to succeed at the job.
If the employer sees that the employee is struggling or making errors, minor or
major, good instruction and supervision will eliminate or minimize these
problems.

[
178
]

The difficulty for Fleet Brake was that Mr. Tipon’s immediate
supervisor after March, 2014 was located in Calgary and Mr. Palma rarely had
any interaction with Mr. Tipon.  There was very little personal contact with Mr.
Tipon.  In fact, from the time of Mr. Johns’ departure, the evidence
established minimal interaction between management and Mr. Tipon.

[
179
]

Mr. Tipon only met with his supervisor, Mr. Palma, on three or four
occasions over 14 months.  It is not surprising, therefore, that no employment
reviews were ever completed by management prior to Mr. Tipon’s dismissal and
that no “feedback” was provided.

[
180
]

For management to complain that the work “could manage itself,” so
as to minimize its involvement, was extremely discourteous and disrespectful to
Mr. Tipon.  Considering how important management insisted Mr. Tipon’s work was
to the company, this amounts to an abdication of its duties as an employer.

[
181
]

I have considered the evidence, in particular the documented
communications presented to me.  It is clear that there was no incompetence or
deception exhibited by the Plaintiff during his employment with the defendant.  At
worst, Mr Tipon was naïve in believing he could get the COR extension.

[
182
]

Mr. Tipon was only advised definitively that a deadline extension would
not be provided on March 27, 2015. In the interim, he had advised his employer,
both in communication with his immediate supervisor and in subsequent emails to
management, that the COR recertification was in jeopardy. This was as early as
September 18, 2014.

[
183
]

It is clear to me that the Defendant repudiated the employment
contract by:

1.

Eliminating the assistance that Mr. Tipon
required in order to meet his responsibilities by dismissing Ms. Jurace in
September, 2014; and

2.

Eliminating the supervision and support Mr. Tipon required in order
to meet his responsibilities by failing to adequately replace Mr. Johns with
competent alternate supervision.

[
184
]

The employer was required to provide adequate
supervision and support  for Mr. Tipon, even if the Plaintiff was not “asking”
for help.  However, Mr. Tipon had in fact pleaded with Mr. Palma not to dismiss
Ms. Jurace, as without her the COR application could be in jeopardy. I view
this as a plea for help and this plea fell on deaf ears.

Can the Defendant
rely on “after acquired cause”?

[
185
]

I would refer the parties to
Nelson
v.
Champion Feed
Services Inc
.,
2010 ABQB 409
[Nelson] in seeking assistance to this
question.  I am not persuaded that there was any after acquired knowledge that
would provide just cause for the termination of the Plaintiff.

[
186
]

Like Graesser, J. in
Nelson
, I find no evidence of dishonesty
and no evidence of dishonest intent.  “At worst, Mr. Nelson did not do his job
properly ... It was a serious error but without any willfulness or bad intend”
(at para. 78).

[
187
]

I find that the employer has failed to discharge its onus in this
regard.  I find the employer did not prove it had grounds to terminate the
Plaintiff’s employment.

Did the
Defendant dismiss the Plaintiff in bad faith?

[
188
]

There is no requirement to give reasons for an employee’s dismissal  (see

Schlosser v Excel Resources Society,
2014 ABPC 369 at para. 55
quoting
Halsburry’s
Laws of England
, 2 ed. Vol. 22 p. 155).

[
189
]

However, on Monday, June 8, 2015, Mr. John Bzeta emailed Mr. Tipon
and stated the following:

“Non-performance was
the reasons for your termination.  I apologize this was not made clearer.”

[
190
]

In a letter sent earlier that day, Mr. Bzeta advised:

“It was my
decision to termination you for cause. ... (Y)ou were terminated for not doing
what was expected of the position ... In summary, I believe Dindo you are a
good person and can be successful in your trade.  However, the mistakes you
made at Fleet Brake could not be corrected.”

[
191
]

On the evidence, the reasons given were inaccurate.  The employer
took no responsibility for what happened.  “The law requires employers to be
candid, reasonable, honest and forthright with their employees.”  Employers
cannot lawfully engage “in conduct that is unfair or is in bad faith by being,
for example, untruthful, misleading or unduly insensitive” (
Wallace
v.

United Grain Growers Inc

2008 SCC 39
at para.
98
).

[
192
]

In
Karmel
v.
Calgary Jewish Academy,

2015 ABQB 731
,
Justice MacLeod referenced two recent Supreme Court of Canada decisions,
Bhasin

v.
Hrynew

2014 SCC 71
, and
Potter
v.
New Brunswick Legal
Aid Services Commission

2015 SCC 10
.

[
193
]

He states at paragraphs 94 and 95 of
Karmel, supra
:

“94
Two recent cases of the Supreme Court of Canada are directly relevant here.
First, in Bhasin v Hrynew,
2014 SCC 71
, the Court was unanimous in recognizing
that "good faith contractual performance is a general organizing principle
of the common law," see para 33. As a result of the decision in Bhasin,
parties to a contract have a duty to act honestly in the performance of their
contractual obligations.

95     While
Bhasin was not specific to the employment context, the Supreme Court's decision
in Potter v New Brunswick Legal Aid Services Commission,
2015 SCC 10
,
referenced the good faith requirements in Bhasin in the context of wrongful
dismissal. The Court defined the employer's duty of good faith as one which
extends throughout the duration of employment, and not just at the time or
event of termination. Employers must therefore demonstrate good faith for the
entirety of the employment contract.”

[
194
]

However, I must determine if the conduct of the employer warrants
aggravated damages in this case.
Fidler
v.
Sunlife Assurance Co of
Canada

2006 SCC 30 (CanLII)
, [2006] SCJ No. 30 clarified the meaning of aggravated damages in
Canada.  In its decision, the Supreme Court cited the definition of “aggravated
damages” adopted in
Vorvis
v.
Insurance Corp of British Columbia

1989 CanLII 93 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 SCR 1085 at para.
16
:

“... aggravated
damages describes an award that aims at compensation but takes full account of
the intangible injuries, such as distress and humiliation, that may have been caused
by the defendant’s insulting behaviour.”

[
195
]

In
Boucher
v.
Wal-Mart Canada Corp

2014 ONCA 419
, the Ontario Court of Appeal upheld an award of aggravated
damaged by holding at para. 66:

“66
Aggravated damages are compensatory damages. They are part of breach of
contract damages. They compensate a plaintiff for the additional harm suffered
because of the way the contract was breached. In a wrongful dismissal claim,
aggravated damages may be awarded against the employer where "the employer
engages in conduct during the course of dismissal that is 'unfair or is in bad
faith'": see Honda Canada Inc. v. Keays,
2008 SCC 39
, [2008] 2 S.C.R. 362,
at para.
57
. However, "the normal distress and hurt feelings resulting
from dismissal are not compensable.":”

[
196
]

In my view, the conduct of Fleet Brake towards Mr. Tipon was not
calculated or directed solely at him, unlike in
Karmel
, supra
.  This was
a case of the employer getting swept up in a “perfect storm” of expansion,
followed by an almost immediate economic contraction.  I believe it is fair and
correct for me to infer that the management of the Defendant was more focused
on cuts in expenses, advancing sales, closing offices and reducing staff than
purposely and callously making Mr. Tipon’s work life miserable.  Their
“reasons” for termination, through clumsy and inaccurate, do not fall within
that class as defined by
Fidler
and
Vorvis.
In my view, the
employer’s conduct did not display the ‘blatant disregard” for Mr. Tipon.  I
would add that “... mere sloppy conduct by the employer does not suffice for
such extra damages, it takes something akin to intent, malice or blatant
disregard to the employee.” (
Merrill Lynch Canada Inc
. v.
Soost

2010 ABCA 251
at para.
17
quoting from
Gismond
v.
Toronto (City)

2003 CanLII 52143 (ON CA)
, 2003 64 O.R. (3d) 688).

[
197
]

I therefore decline to award aggravated damages to Mr. Tipon.

NOTICE PERIOD

[
198
]

Having regard to all the factors, I conclude that a reasonable
notice period is 6 months.

DAMAGES

[
199
]

Mr. Tipon is entitled to damages in lieu of notice.

[
200
]

The factors to consider are set out in
Bardal
v.
Globe and
Mail Ltd
,
1960 CanLII 294 (ON HCJ)
, [1960] O.J. 149:

“21     There can be no
catalogue laid down as to what is reasonable notice in particular classes of
cases. The reasonableness of the notice must be decided with reference to each
particular case, having regard to the character of the employment, the length
of service of the servant, the age of the servant and the availability of
similar employment, having regard to the experience, training and
qualifications of the servant.”

[
201
]

To Mr. Tipon’s credit, he was able to find new employment in 4.5
months post dismissal. This was during very difficult economic times. I am
satisfied that this was reasonable mitigation in this case.

[
202
]

Mr. Tipon’s new job pays him $57,000.00 per year, or $4,750.00 per
month.  His salary with the Defendant was $6,866.00 per month. This creates a
difference of $2,116.00 per month for the 1.5 months while he was re-employed
during the notice period.

[
203
]

Given that the Defendant provided the Plaintiff with one months’
notice, credit for $6,866.00 is to be given. A further adjustment must be made
for the period of notice during which Mr. Tipon was re-employed. He is awarded
the difference between his salaries during that period.

[
204
]

I will further award a global amount of $1,500.00 in loss of health
and other collateral benefits during the 6 month notice period.  However, as no
evidence was led regarding the payment of a bonus for the year of dismissal
(2015), I decline to order any amount in that regard.

[
205
]

Judgment is awarded to the Plaintiff as follows:

Six months wages in lieu of
dismissal:                                   $41,200.00

Six months benefits

$1,500.00

$42,700.00

Credit for one Months’ Notice                       ($6,866.00)

Credit for 1 ½ months’ alternate
income
($7,125.00)

$13,991.00

TOTAL:                                                                                 $28,709.00

[
206
]

Judgment Interest from May 27, 2015 is also granted.

[
207
]

Judgment is awarded in this amount.  Costs shall also be awarded and
I am directing Counsel to submit a written summary of submissions within 30
days of this Judgment if they cannot agree as to costs.

[
208
]

I thank Counsel for their assistance in this case.
